evidence.claim: The International Selkirk Loop circles the Selkirk Mountains through Washington, Idaho and British Columbia over 280 miles.
evidence.quote: a 450 km / 280-mile scenic drive encircling the spectacular Selkirk Mountains of Washington , Idaho and British Columbia

evidence.claim: The U.S. portion is an All-American Road.
evidence.quote: The portion of the loop in the United States has been designated an All-American Road

evidence.claim: Washington State Tourism highlights forest walks, river views and small towns; Visit Idaho describes nearly its entire section as following rivers and lakeshores.
evidence.quote: With nearly the entire Idaho portion following crystal-clear rivers and lakeshores

evidence.claim: The Kootenay Lake ferry forms part of the circuit.
evidence.quote: Included on the loop is the Kootenay Lake Ferry

evidence.claim: Washington State Tourism highlights forest walks, river views and small towns
evidence.quote: North of Spokane, hike through vast forests, enjoy river views, and stop by small towns.

evidence.claim: The Washington border connection developed in stages.
evidence.quote: this particular crossing did not exist until the Pend Oreille Highway was completed in 1921.

evidence.claim: Completion of the Pend Oreille Highway in 1921 created the crossing at Nelway; the British Columbia highway officially opened in 1923.
evidence.quote: this particular crossing did not exist until the Pend Oreille Highway was completed in 1921. The highway on the BC side officially opened in 1923

evidence.claim: Its narrow, winding surface drew criticism, and realignment and paving began in 1948.
evidence.quote: The British Columbia section of the highway faced criticism for many years due to its narrow, winding, and rough terrain, making travel slow and difficult. To handle increasing traffic, sections were progressively realigned and paved from 1948

evidence.claim: The scenic loop received All-American Road designation in 2005.
evidence.quote: Designated as an All-American Road in 2005

evidence.claim: Starting at Metaline Falls, travel south past Ione and Tiger toward Usk.
evidence.quote: State Route 31 passes through Metaline Falls, connecting the town to the rest of the state highway system at Tiger in the south and with Canada at Nelway, British Columbia.

evidence.claim: Across the border, the circuit continues through Creston, along Kootenay Lake and across the lake by ferry.
evidence.quote: The ferry is approximately 5.4 miles (8.7 km) in length, and connects the loop to the eastern shore of the lake.

evidence.claim: Nelson and Salmo complete the Canadian arc before the return through Nelway to Washington.
evidence.quote: The route proceeds through the community of Salmo before proceeding northeast.

evidence.claim: south past Ione and Tiger toward Usk
evidence.quote: It proceeds north, passing through a small portion of Colville National Forest, before entering Ione.

evidence.claim: Tiger
evidence.quote: 3.5 miles (5.6 km) south of Ione

evidence.claim: through Sandpoint and Bonners Ferry to Porthill
evidence.quote: From Oldtown, head north on U.S. Route 2 through Sandpoint towards Bonners Ferry. Continue north on U.S. Route 95, take the left fork onto the 1 to the Canadian border and cross the Idaho-Canada border in Porthill.

evidence.claim: through Creston, along Kootenay Lake
evidence.quote: The road passes through Crawford Bay before bending south and traveling along one of the arms of the lake.

evidence.claim: through Creston
evidence.quote: The road enters Creston

evidence.claim: Nelson
evidence.quote: In Nelson, the Loop's designation transfers to British Columbia Highway 3A

evidence.claim: return through Nelway to Washington
evidence.quote: The Metaline Falls–Nelway Border Crossing connects the town of Metaline Falls, Washington with Nelway and Nelson, British Columbia at the Canada–US border.

evidence.claim: At Metaline Falls, the Pend Oreille River turns east to get past Washington Rock before continuing toward Canada.
evidence.quote: The river makes a zig zag at Metaline Falls, turning briefly to the east to get around Washington Rock

evidence.claim: The town developed with lead and zinc mining, then gained a railroad connection in 1910 and a cement plant drawing on local limestone.
evidence.quote: Then in 1910, Metaline Falls was connected with the Idaho and Washington Northern Railroad.  The Lehigh Portland Cement Co. plant was soon built, taking advantage of the region's limestone deposits.

evidence.claim: One building has made a different transition.
evidence.quote: which is now known as the Cutter Theater and serves as a community center.

evidence.claim: Kirtland Cutter designed the 1912 school in the classical revival style.
evidence.quote: The Metaline Falls School, also designed by Cutter, was built in 1912 in the classical revival style.

evidence.claim: After its abandonment in 1972, residents organized to care for it in 1990; the former school now serves as the Cutter Theater and community center.
evidence.quote: The school was abandoned in 1972 and sat unmaintained until 1990 when local residents came together to take care of the historic building, which is now known as the Cutter Theater and serves as a community center.

evidence.claim: The town developed with lead and zinc mining
evidence.quote: The settlement of Metaline Falls was founded in 1900, with most of its residents then employed by the Mammoth and Morning lead-zinc mines.

evidence.claim: Tiger began at a river landing established by George Tiger in 1899.
evidence.quote: Tiger had its start in 1899 when George Tiger established a river landing there.

evidence.claim: The community stands on the west bank of the north-flowing Pend Oreille.
evidence.quote: Tiger is located on the west bank of the Pend Oreille River as it flows north towards British Columbia, Canada.

evidence.claim: At the junction of highways 20 and 31, its 1913 store and post office now houses the Tiger Historical Center and Museum.
evidence.quote: Located at the junction of highways 20 and 31, Tiger is the start of the North Pend Oreille Scenic Byway. Open seasonally, the Tiger Historical Center and Museum is housed in a 1913 former store and post office.

evidence.claim: Washington State Tourism identifies it as the community’s only remaining building.
evidence.quote: Today, it’s the only building that remains of this community.

evidence.claim: A ferry gave Bonners Ferry its name, but flooding shaped its streets.
evidence.quote: Bonners Ferry, perched on stilts to avoid the inevitable spring floods, appeared to be a boom town.

evidence.claim: Edwin Bonner started the crossing in 1864 where the Wildhorse Trail met the Kootenai River, serving the route to British Columbia’s goldfields.
evidence.quote: Edwin Bonner, a merchant from Walla Walla, Washington, established a ferry in 1864 where the trail crossed the broad Kootenai River.

evidence.claim: Richard Fry and his Sinixt wife, Justine Su-steel Fry, leased the ferry in 1875; Bonner’s name remained.
evidence.quote: In 1875, Richard Fry, and his Sinixt wife, Justine Su-steel Fry, leased the business, but the location retained the name of the original founder

evidence.claim: The growing town raised buildings on stilts against spring floods.
evidence.quote: Bonners Ferry, perched on stilts to avoid the inevitable spring floods

evidence.claim: Later, levees and brick construction changed downtown, and much of Main Street dates from that period of permanent building.
evidence.quote: Today, much of Main Street dates from this initial period of solid, permanent construction.

evidence.claim: serving the route to British Columbia’s goldfields
evidence.quote: When gold was discovered in the East Kootenays of British Columbia in 1863, thousands of prospectors from all over the West surged northward over a route that became known as the Wildhorse Trail.

evidence.claim: Later, levees and brick construction changed downtown
evidence.quote: The valley land was drained, levees were constructed

evidence.claim: brick construction
evidence.quote: The downtown took shape as brick buildings were constructed, replacing those on stilts.

evidence.claim: In Idaho, the loop joins two existing scenic byways: Wild Horse Trail and Panhandle Historic Rivers Passage.
evidence.quote: The International Selkirk Loop connects two Idaho scenic byways— Wild Horse Trail Scenic Byway and Panhandle Historic Rivers Passage .

evidence.claim: Near Usk, the road passes the Kalispel Tribe of Indians reservation. Washington State Tourism notes that travelers on LeClerc Road may spot the tribe’s bison herd grazing in the distance.
evidence.quote: The Kalispel Tribe of Indians reservation lies along the Pend Oreille River near Usk. As you travel LeClerc Road, you may spot the tribe’s bison herd grazing in the distance.

evidence.claim: Continue through Newport at the Idaho border.
evidence.quote: Set along the Idaho border, Newport serves as the starting point for the Washington segment

evidence.claim: The Idaho leg runs through Sandpoint and Bonners Ferry to Porthill.
evidence.quote: From Oldtown, head north on U.S. Route 2 through Sandpoint towards Bonners Ferry. Continue north on U.S. Route 95, take the left fork onto the 1 to the Canadian border and cross the Idaho-Canada border in Porthill.

evidence.claim: Washington Rock towers immediately north of the town and its river bridge.
evidence.quote: Washington Rock, which towers over Metaline Falls immediately to the north of the town and the Metaline Falls Bridge.

evidence.claim: Completion of Libby Dam in 1975 reduced the threat of serious flooding.
evidence.quote: Completion of the Libby Dam in 1975 lessened the threat of serious flooding.

evidence.claim: travel south past Ione and Tiger toward Usk
evidence.quote: The road continues, intersecting several small roads before entering the community of Usk
